before: A hash collection uses equality to decide whether values represent the same key. A record automatically supplies value equality for its data, unlike ordinary class reference equality by default.
Do not mutate fields used by equality or hashing while a key is stored in a hash collection. The record key here is used unchanged. Hash codes are not durable IDs or cryptographic fingerprints.
Expected behavior from this example: 1. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer: Compare two equal records with two new ordinary class instances. Explain why customizing equality also requires compatible hashing. This is a separate local practice task, not a requirement to mark the reading complete.
after: Equality decides whether two values count as the same. This record compares its Name data, so separate TopicKey objects can be equal.
A hash code is a number used to help a collection find a value. GetHashCode returns it. Equals decides logical equality; a matching hash alone does not prove equality.
Equal values must have equal hash codes during the same run. Different values may also share a hash, called a collision. This record supplies compatible equality and hashing automatically.
The program prints 1. Both TopicKey records contain the same name, C#, so the set keeps one distinct value.

Do not change data used for equality or hashing while a key is stored in a hash collection. Hash codes are not permanent identifiers or secure fingerprints. This example leaves its record keys unchanged.

before.question: Change only second to new TopicKey("Python"). What count should be printed?
choices: 1 because every record of the same type is equal
2 because these record values have different names
It depends only on whether their hash codes collide
before.explanation: Record equality compares the data here. C# and Python are different names, so the set retains both even if hashes ever collide.

after.question: Make second a TopicKey with the name "Python" instead. What Count prints?
choices: It depends only on whether the hashes collide
after.explanation: The names differ, so the records are unequal. The set keeps both, even if their hashes happened to match.
